newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - US, Europe get a dose of dollar power.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - US, Europe get a dose of dollar power.

text.p: Spirited gains in the U.S. dollar have formed a major prop for recent rallies in Treasuries and European high-yielders and will continue to offer support until the end of the year, international economists said on Friday.
With dollar strength pushing a wave of funds out of Asia and into U.S. Treasuries, analysts said investors can pick up good gains by hitching a ride.
"Japanese investors are getting ridiculously low returns in domestic bond and equity markets and are being forced into overseas markets," said Nikko Europe's Stuart Thomson in London.
"The dollar rally reflets that demand for overseas assets."
Within Europe, the smart money should head for the short-end of high-yielding debt markets, analysts said.
There, a stronger dollar will allow domestic currencies to appreciate against the mark, tightening monetary conditions, helping to tame inflation and opening the way for official interest rate cuts.

"The dollar's move is very good news for the short end of some of the European markets, particularly Italian and Spanish bonds," said Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

The Bank of Italy cut its official discount rate to 7.5 percent last week from 8.25 percent, and analysts said with the lira now trading stronger than the psychological 1,000 level against the mark, more easings are on the cards.

In Spain, where the central bank last cut its repo rate by 50 basis points to 6.75 percent in early October, the government has said any further monetary easing this year will depend on inflation, currently at 3.6 percent.
McDevitt said the pivot level for gains in high-yielding bonds was 1.52 on dollar/mark, and a sustained break above there would offer good support for short-dated paper.

The dollar was at 1.5182/89 marks and 113.76/82 yen by 1155 GMT. Dollar/mark gained more than eight pfennigs from end-July to mid-October but has since given back more than two pfennigs. The dollar has risen more than seven yen since July 31.

"If the dollar does sustain that move, it will keep the convergence theme in Europe going," said McDevitt. "Bond markets overall will do well, but it will be particularly positive for the short end of high-yielders."
Thomson, Nikko's chief international economist, said that for those who prefer the heavyweight bond markets, the 10-year yield gap between U.S. and Japanese bonds will offer rewards.
"One of the triggers for the rally in U.S. Teasuries over the past two months was a move to 400 basis points on the 10-year Japan/U.S. yield spread," he said.
The gap is now around 391 basis points, but Thomson said T-bond buyers will profit as it slims further. "That spread can certainly come in to 375, possibly even 350 basis points," said Thomson.

Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at Natwest Capital markets in London, also noted the recent fund flows into Treasuries and said dollar strength coupled with a positive technical outlook should ensure T-bonds will outpeform core European markets in the short term.
Recent enthusiasm for U.S. debt has pushed the T-note/Bund spread to a current 46 basis points from highs around 70 in recent weeks, and Roberts forecast more gains for Treasury investors.
"We're going to see that spread narrow further," he said. "Down to 40 or even 35 basis points is possible."

While analysts said the dollar's strength looked relatively solid over the medium term, they said a few blips between now and the end of the year may halt its rise, risking temporary fallout in European bond markets.

"There is some concern that the Democrats may win both houses of Congress in the elections and that this would be inflationary," said Thomson. "But I think that would cause no more than a pause in the dollar rally."
-- Kate Kelland, International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 8682
